title: MIT 6.858: Web Security Model & Securing Web Apps
summary: The browser's security model from first principles: the same-origin policy, how cross-site scripting and CSRF break it, SQL injection and parameterized defenses, and session management done right. You finish by finding and fixing real vulnerabilities in OWASP Juice Shop.
objectives: Explain the same-origin policy in terms of scheme, host, and port, and what it does and does not isolate.
Distinguish reflected, stored, and DOM-based XSS, and apply output encoding, CSP, and HttpOnly as defenses.
Describe how CSRF exploits ambient authority and apply synchronizer tokens and SameSite cookies to stop it.
Explain SQL injection conceptually and defend with parameterized queries and least-privilege database accounts.
Design session management that resists fixation and hijacking: secure randomness, rotation, cookie flags, timeouts.

notes.title: The web security model: origins and the same-origin policy
notes.body: An origin is the triple (scheme, host, port). https://bank.example:443 and https://bank.example:8443 are different origins; https://bank.example and http://bank.example are different origins; https://app.bank.example and https://bank.example are different origins. The same-origin policy (SOP) is the browser's core isolation rule: a script running in one origin cannot read the DOM, cookies, localStorage, or fetch responses of another origin. Without it, any page you visit could read your webmail. Worked example: you are logged into webmail at https://mail.example. You open an attacker's page at https://evil.example in another tab. The attacker's JavaScript runs fetch('https://mail.example/inbox'). The browser sends the request (your mail cookies go along, because cookies attach by destination domain), but the SOP blocks the evil page from reading the response. The attacker's script gets a network error, not your inbox. Reading is blocked; sending is not. That asymmetry is the source of half of web security: CSRF exploits the sending side, XSS defeats the reading side by running inside the victim origin. notes.title: Cross-site scripting: reflected, stored, and DOM-based
notes.body: XSS happens when attacker-controlled input becomes executable script in a victim's browser, inside the victim origin — which means the script inherits the victim origin's privileges: it can read the DOM, fire authenticated requests, and exfiltrate data. Reflected XSS: the payload arrives in a request and is echoed into the response. Worked example: a search page renders results with echo 'Results for: ' + q, where q comes from the URL query string. The attacker crafts https://shop.example/search?q= and tricks a victim into clicking. The server reflects the script into the page, the victim's browser executes it in the shop origin, and the cookie goes to the attacker. The fix is output encoding for the context: HTML-encode <, >, &, quotes when injecting into HTML body. Stored XSS: the payload is saved server-side and served to every viewer. Worked example: a comment field stores raw HTML; the attacker posts as a product review. Every shopper who views the product executes it. Stored XSS is worse than reflected because no per-victim trick is needed — the application delivers the attack itself. Same fix, applied at render time (encode on output, not on input, because the same data may be rendered in HTML, JS, and URL contexts needing different encodings). DOM-based XSS: the vulnerability lives entirely in client-side JavaScript. Worked example: a page does element.innerHTML = location.hash.slice(1) to render a welcome message from the URL fragment. The fragment never reaches the server, so server-side filters miss it; the attack URL is https://shop.example/welcome#. Defense: never sink untrusted data into innerHTML; use textContent, or a sanitizer for the rare cases rich HTML is required. Defense in depth: HttpOnly on session cookies keeps stolen-script from reading document.cookie (it can still act as the user, so this is mitigation, not a fix); Content Security Policy (script-src allowlists) can neuter injected scripts in modern browsers. notes.title: Cross-site request forgery: exploiting ambient authority
notes.body:
CSRF exploits the asymmetry noted earlier: the browser attaches cookies to cross-origin requests automatically, so a malicious page can make your browser issue authenticated requests you never intended.

Worked example: you are logged into https://bank.example. You visit https://evil.example, which contains <form action="https://bank.example/transfer" method="POST"> with hidden fields to=attacker&amount=1000, plus a script that auto-submits it. Your browser sends the POST with your bank session cookie. The bank sees a valid session and performs the transfer. You never clicked anything at the bank. Classic CSRF targets state-changing GETs and simple POSTs; modern variants also target JSON APIs via form-encoded fallbacks and login CSRF.

Why the SOP does not stop this: the SOP blocks reading the response, but the damage (the transfer) happens server-side regardless of whether the attacker reads the response. CSRF is a write-side attack.

Defenses, layered. First, the synchronizer token pattern: the server embeds an unguessable token in each form (and the page's JavaScript for AJAX); the server rejects state-changing requests lacking the token. The attacker's page is cross-origin, so it cannot read the token from the bank's pages (SOP blocks the read), and cannot guess it. Second, SameSite cookies: marking the session cookie SameSite=Lax or Strict tells the browser not to attach it on cross-site requests at all — Lax is the modern default in browsers and kills classic CSRF, though top-level GET navigations still carry Lax cookies, so keep state changes off GET. Third, verify the Origin or Referer header on state-changing endpoints as a backstop. Common mistakes: putting the CSRF token in a cookie instead of the body (the attacker doesn't need to read it if it's auto-attached — the token must travel in a channel the attacker cannot trigger, i.e., request body/header, and must be tied to the session); exempting 'safe' endpoints that actually change state; and assuming SameSite=None is needed for legitimate embedded flows without understanding it re-opens CSRF.

Two CSRF variants deserve special mention. Login CSRF: the attacker forges a login to the victim's browser using the attacker's own credentials — the victim then unknowingly acts inside the attacker's account (uploading sensitive documents into it, for example). The synchronizer-token defense applies to login forms too, which teams often forget. Second, the double-submit cookie pattern: the server sets a random token in a cookie and requires the same value in a request header or body field; the attacker's cross-origin page can't read the cookie value (SOP) so it can't echo it. It's weaker than server-side synchronizer tokens (it fails if any subdomain can write cookies — cookie tossing), but it's stateless and better than nothing. And a cookie-flag subtlety: cross-site legitimate flows (embedded checkout widgets) that genuinely need cookies must use SameSite=None; Secure together — None without Secure is rejected by modern browsers. Audit for SameSite=None cookies and ask of each one: is this cross-site flow real, and is the endpoint CSRF-protected anyway?

notes.title: SQL injection: concept and the parameterized defense
notes.body:
SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a SQL string, so the input is parsed as code. The database cannot tell which parts of the query the developer wrote and which parts the attacker supplied.

Worked example: a login form builds query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + username + "' AND pass='" + password + "'". A normal login with username enmanuel produces ...WHERE name='enmanuel' AND pass='...'. An attacker enters username: ' OR '1'='1 and any password. The query becomes ...WHERE name='' OR '1'='1' AND pass='...'. Because '1'='1' is always true, the WHERE clause matches rows it shouldn't, and the attacker logs in as the first user in the table — often an administrator. Variants: UNION-based extraction (append UNION SELECT to read other tables), and blind SQLi, where no data is returned directly and the attacker asks yes/no questions through timing or boolean responses to exfiltrate data one bit at a time.

The defense is parameterized queries (prepared statements): the SQL structure is sent to the database first, with placeholders, and the user values are sent separately as data, never parsed as SQL. In Python's sqlite3: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name=?", (username,)) — the ? placeholder means username can contain quotes, semicolons, anything, and it is still just a string value. Every mature database driver supports this; there is no legitimate reason to concatenate input into queries.

Layered habits: run the application database account with least privilege (a web app account that can only SELECT/INSERT on its own tables cannot DROP the schema even if an injection slips through); never expose raw database errors to users (error text teaches attackers the schema); and treat stored procedures and ORMs as helpers, not guarantees — an ORM used with raw string queries is just as injectable. Operator gotcha: input 'sanitization' by escaping quotes is fragile across encodings and database quirks; parameterization is the fix, escaping is a hope.

Watch for second-order SQL injection, the variant that survives naive review: the payload is stored safely the first time (properly parameterized on insert), but later retrieved and concatenated into a different query without parameters. The injection fires on read, not on write — input validation at the door doesn't help because the dangerous moment is a query the reviewer didn't trace. The fix is the same (parameters everywhere), but finding it requires tracing data flow, not just entry points. On ORMs: they parameterize the queries they generate, but every ORM offers an escape hatch for raw SQL — audit each raw() / execute() call as if the ORM weren't there. And on web application firewalls: a WAF that blocks suspicious strings is a tripwire, not a fix — it raises the attacker's effort and logs attempts, but bypasses are routine. Never let 'the WAF handles it' substitute for parameterized queries; the day someone misconfigures the WAF, the vulnerability is still sitting in your code.

notes.title: Session management: fixation, hijacking, and cookie flags
notes.body:
HTTP is stateless, so applications track logged-in users with a session identifier, usually a cookie. Whoever holds the identifier is treated as the user — so the identifier must be unguessable, protected in transit and storage, and invalidated properly.

Session fixation: the attacker sets the victim's session id before login, then uses it after. Worked example: the app accepts a session id from a URL parameter. The attacker sends the victim a link with ?sessionid=ATTACKERKNOWN. The victim logs in; the server keeps the same id and now associates it with the victim's account. The attacker, knowing the id, browses as the victim. Defense: generate a fresh, cryptographically random session id at login (regenerate on privilege change), and never accept session ids from URLs.

Session hijacking: stealing the id via XSS (HttpOnly blunts this), network sniffing (TLS everywhere blunts this — see M18), or malware. Defenses in depth: 128+ bits of entropy from a cryptographic RNG; Secure flag (cookie sent only over HTTPS); HttpOnly (invisible to JavaScript); SameSite=Lax or Strict (not sent cross-site); absolute plus idle timeouts (e.g., expire after 8 hours regardless, and after 30 minutes idle); and server-side invalidation on logout and on password change (log me out everywhere).

Worked design: on successful login the server calls a secure random generator for a 256-bit id, stores (id -> user, created_at, last_seen) server-side, sets Set-Cookie: session=<id>; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/, and rotates the id on privilege escalation. On each request it checks expiry and updates last_seen. On logout it deletes the server-side record. Common mistakes: predictable ids (timestamps, usernames, sequential numbers); sessions that never expire ('remember me' implemented as a permanent session id instead of a separate, rotatable long-lived token); and trusting the client clock or client-stored roles.

Design 'remember me' as a separate mechanism from sessions, because conflating them creates permanent session ids. The sound pattern: on opt-in, generate a long random token, store only its hash server-side bound to the user and device fingerprint, set it in a Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite cookie with a long expiry (e.g., 30 days), and on use, mint a fresh short-lived session id and rotate the remember-me token itself. Theft of the cookie then buys at most one session, and rotation invalidates the stolen copy. Also consider concurrent-session policy: for sensitive apps, limit active sessions per user and surface 'active sessions' in account settings with remote-revoke — users spotting an unknown session is a detection source you get for free. Finally, bind sessions to sensible context without overdoing it: strict IP binding breaks legitimate mobile users (carrier NAT, network hops), so prefer risk signals (impossible travel, new device) that step up to re-authentication rather than hard-binding that punishes normal behavior.

notes.title: Clickjacking, security headers, and defense in depth
notes.body:
Clickjacking (UI redressing) tricks the user into clicking something different from what they perceive. Worked example: the attacker embeds the bank's 'confirm transfer' page in a transparent iframe positioned exactly under a fake 'Claim your prize' button. The victim clicks the visible button; the click lands on the bank's confirm control inside the invisible iframe, and the victim's session authorizes the transfer. The fix is framing control: the X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGIN header, or the modern Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive, tells the browser which origins may embed the page. Sensitive actions additionally deserve a confirmation step that cannot be iframed away.

Security headers are cheap, global mitigations you set once: Content-Security-Policy (restrict where scripts, styles, images, and frames may load from — a tight script-src policy neuters most XSS payloads even when an injection bug exists); Strict-Transport-Security (covered deeply in M18 — forces HTTPS); X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff (stops browsers from MIME-sniffing a text upload into executable script); Referrer-Policy (limits sensitive URL leakage in the Referer header). None of these fixes a vulnerability, but each shrinks what a vulnerability can be turned into — that is defense in depth.

Threat-model the app before you harden it: enumerate trust boundaries (browser vs server, user vs admin, your origin vs third-party scripts), then ask per boundary what an attacker with the adjacent position can do. Third-party JavaScript deserves special suspicion: every analytics, chat, or ad script runs with your origin's full privileges — a compromised vendor script is stored XSS you installed yourself. Subresource Integrity (SRI) hashes let you pin the exact bytes you expect. Operator habit: when you inherit a web app, read its response headers and its third-party script list before you read its code.

Two more headers earn their place in your baseline. Subresource Integrity (SRI): for third-party scripts you must embed, add an integrity hash — the browser refuses to execute bytes that don't match, so a compromised CDN or vendor can't turn your embed into their payload. Generate the hash from the exact file you vetted and pin the version; auto-updating 'latest' URLs defeat SRI's purpose. Permissions-Policy (formerly Feature-Policy): restricts powerful browser features (camera, microphone, geolocation) by origin — your marketing page has no business accessing the camera, so say so explicitly and a compromised script can't either. Your audit checklist for any inherited app: fetch the response headers and confirm CSP (ideally nonce-based), HSTS, X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors, nosniff, Referrer-Policy, and Permissions-Policy; list every third-party script with its SRI status; and verify the app doesn't frame-bust with JavaScript alone (frame-busting scripts are bypassable — headers are the enforcement). Headers are the cheapest defense-in-depth you'll ever deploy.

notes.title: Secure-by-default habits for builders and operators
notes.body:
Most web vulnerabilities are not exotic; they are defaults that were never changed. Build the habit of secure defaults and you prevent entire bug classes.

Input handling: validate against an allowlist (this field must match this pattern) rather than a denylist (block these bad strings). Denylists fail because attackers are creative and encodings are many; allowlists fail closed. Validate on the server — client-side validation is UX, not security, because the attacker sends raw HTTP. Worked example: an avatar upload that checks only the file extension allows evil.jpg.php or a polyglot; checking the actual content type, re-encoding the image, storing it outside the web root, and serving it with Content-Disposition: attachment defeats the whole class.

Authentication and authorization: require authentication by default and carve out public routes explicitly, not the reverse. Check authorization on every request, not just by hiding links — forced browsing (guessing /admin/users/123) defeats UI-only hiding. Use the platform's session and crypto libraries; hand-rolled crypto and hand-rolled session ids are where breaches are born.

Logging and errors: log authentication failures, authorization denials, and input-validation rejections with enough context (time, source, account, endpoint) to reconstruct an attack, but never log passwords, tokens, or full session ids. Show users generic errors ('login failed') while logging specifics server-side.

Dependency hygiene: the average app ships hundreds of transitive dependencies; a known-vulnerable library is a known-open door. Track them, patch them, and prefer small, well-maintained ones. This is the operator's bridge to the rest of IL-29: allowlisting (M-series on ThreatLocker) constrains what code may run, network control constrains where it may talk, and the economics module (M22) explains why patching lags and how to argue for the budget to fix it.

Make threat modeling a habit, not a ceremony. The lightweight version that actually gets used: for each feature, name the trust boundaries it crosses (anonymous user to authenticated, user to admin, your origin to third-party, app to database), then walk STRIDE per boundary — Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. A comment feature: spoofing (can I post as someone else?), tampering (can I edit others' comments?), information disclosure (does the error leak e-mails?). Fifteen minutes per feature catches the design flaws that code review later finds expensive. Feed the results into your backlog as security requirements, not vague concerns. And culturally: the teams that ship secure defaults have security champions embedded — developers who've taken modules like this one and review designs early. Your career angle: being the person who asks 'what's the trust boundary here?' in design reviews is how junior operators become the team's security voice long before any title change.

cards.front: What three parts make up a web origin?
cards.back: Scheme, host, and port — e.g. https, bank.example, 443.

cards.front: What does the same-origin policy block, and what does it allow?
cards.back: Blocks cross-origin READS (DOM, cookies, fetch responses); still allows cross-origin sends and embedding.

cards.front: Reflected vs stored vs DOM-based XSS?
cards.back: Reflected: payload in request, echoed in response. Stored: saved server-side, served to all viewers. DOM-based: client-side JS sinks untrusted data into the page.

cards.front: What is the correct XSS fix, and where is it applied?
cards.back: Context-appropriate output encoding, applied at render time (on output, per sink context).

cards.front: How does CSRF work in one sentence?
cards.back: The browser auto-attaches cookies to a cross-origin request, so a malicious page can trigger authenticated state-changing actions.

cards.front: Two primary CSRF defenses?
cards.back: Synchronizer (anti-CSRF) tokens in the request body/header, and SameSite=Lax/Strict session cookies.

cards.front: What is SQL injection, fundamentally?
cards.back: User input concatenated into a SQL string so it is parsed as code instead of treated as data.

cards.front: The definitive SQL injection defense?
cards.back: Parameterized queries (prepared statements): structure and data sent separately; input is never parsed as SQL.

cards.front: What is session fixation and its fix?
cards.back: Attacker sets the victim's session id pre-login, then reuses it. Fix: generate a fresh cryptographically random id at login; never accept ids from URLs.

cards.front: What do the Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite cookie flags do?
cards.back: Secure: HTTPS only. HttpOnly: invisible to JavaScript. SameSite: not attached on cross-site requests.

cards.front: What stops clickjacking?
cards.back: X-Frame-Options (DENY/SAMEORIGIN) or CSP frame-ancestors controlling which origins may embed the page.

cards.front: Allowlist vs denylist input validation — which, and why?
cards.back: Allowlist: define what is acceptable. Denylists fail against attacker creativity and encoding tricks; allowlists fail closed.

quiz.q: https://a.example and https://a.example:8443 are…
choices: The same origin if DNS matches
quiz.explain: Origin = scheme + host + port. Any one differing means a different origin, so the SOP treats them as mutually untrusted.

quiz.q: An attacker's page runs fetch('https://mail.example/inbox') while you are logged into webmail. What happens?
choices: The request goes with your cookies but the script cannot read the response
The request is blocked from being sent at all
The script reads your inbox freely
The browser deletes your mail cookies
quiz.explain: The SOP blocks cross-origin reads, not sends. Cookies attach by destination domain, so the request is authenticated — but the evil page can't see the response. This send/receive asymmetry is exactly what CSRF exploits.

quiz.q: A comment system stores raw HTML and renders it to all visitors. An attacker posts . This is…
quiz.explain: The payload persists server-side and executes for every viewer — stored XSS, the most dangerous flavor because victims need no trick link.

quiz.q: A page sets el.innerHTML = location.hash.slice(1). The fragment never reaches the server. This vulnerability is…
quiz.explain: The sink is client-side JavaScript and the source never touches the server — DOM-based XSS. Server-side filters can't see it; fix it in the JS (textContent, never innerHTML with untrusted data).

quiz.q: Why must an anti-CSRF token travel in the request body or a custom header rather than in a cookie?
choices: Cookies are auto-attached cross-origin, so a cookie token proves nothing
Bodies are encrypted and cookies aren't
Custom headers are required by the SOP
quiz.explain: The whole attack is that the browser attaches cookies automatically. A token in a cookie rides along with the forged request. In the body/header, only a page that can read the real site (same-origin) can supply it.

quiz.q: Login query: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + u + "' AND pass='" + p + "'". Input u = ' OR '1'='1. What is the effect?
choices: The WHERE clause becomes always-true and authentication is bypassed
The query fails with a syntax error
Only the password check is skipped
The database deletes the users table
quiz.explain: The injected OR '1'='1' makes the condition true for every row, so the query returns a user (typically the first, often admin) without a valid password. Parameterized queries prevent this entirely.

quiz.q: Which single change most completely fixes SQL injection?
choices: Blocking the word SELECT in input
quiz.explain: Parameters separate code from data at the protocol level — input is never parsed as SQL. Escaping and blacklists are bypassable; hiding errors only slows attackers.

quiz.q: An app accepts ?sessionid= in the URL and keeps it across login. The risk is…
choices: Session fixation — regenerate a fresh random id at login
quiz.explain: An attacker can plant a known session id in the victim's browser before login, then reuse it after. The fix is server-generated cryptographically random ids, rotated at login, never taken from URLs.

quiz.q: A payment page is embedded invisibly under a fake prize button. This attack and its fix:
quiz.explain: UI redressing: the victim's click lands on the hidden sensitive control. Framing headers let the page declare it must not be embedded by attacker origins.

quiz.q: An app validates uploads by checking the file extension only. Why is this insufficient?
choices: Extension checks are denylists; content must be validated, re-encoded, stored outside the web root
It slows down uploads too much
quiz.explain: Extensions are attacker-controlled metadata. Validate the actual content, re-encode it, store outside the web root, and serve with safe headers — allowlist thinking, fail closed.

items.prompt: Name the three components of an origin.
items.answer: Scheme, host, port.
items.explain: All three must match for two URLs to be same-origin.

items.prompt: SOP: does it block the request or the response read for cross-origin fetch?
items.answer: It blocks reading the response; the request (with cookies) still goes.
items.explain: This send-vs-read asymmetry is the root of CSRF.

items.prompt: Which XSS type persists server-side?
items.answer: Stored XSS.
items.explain: Saved once, executed for every viewer — no per-victim lure needed.

items.prompt: Which XSS type never reaches the server?
items.answer: DOM-based XSS.
items.explain: Source (e.g., location.hash) flows into a JS sink like innerHTML entirely client-side.

items.prompt: Correct sink for untrusted text in the DOM?
items.answer: textContent (never innerHTML).
items.explain: textContent treats data as text; innerHTML parses it as markup.

items.prompt: What does the HttpOnly flag protect against, and what does it NOT stop?
items.answer: Stops JS from reading the cookie (blunts XSS theft); does not stop the script from acting as the user.
items.explain: HttpOnly is mitigation, not a fix — injected script still rides the session.

items.prompt: The one-line SQLi fix?
items.answer: Parameterized queries / prepared statements.
items.explain: Structure and data travel separately; input is never parsed as SQL.

items.prompt: Scenario: every visitor's browser fires requests to evil.example after viewing a forum thread. Diagnosis and fix?
items.answer: Stored XSS in the thread renderer; output-encode on render and add CSP.
items.explain: Self-propagating across viewers = stored. Encode for the sink context at output time.

items.prompt: Scenario: state-changing requests arrive at /transfer with valid sessions but no CSRF token, from users who only visited a third-party site. Diagnosis and fix?
items.answer: CSRF; require synchronizer tokens and set SameSite=Lax/Strict on the session cookie.
items.explain: Authenticated requests the user never intended, triggered cross-origin — classic CSRF.

items.prompt: Scenario: login accepts username admin'-- and any password. Diagnosis and fix?
items.answer: SQL injection via string concatenation; switch to parameterized queries and least-privilege DB accounts.
items.explain: '-- comments out the password check. Parameters eliminate the class.

items.prompt: Scenario: support staff report sessions that never expire, and 'remember me' is a permanent session id cookie. What's wrong?
items.answer: No absolute timeout; permanent session ids. Use short sessions plus a separate rotatable remember-me token.
items.explain: A stolen permanent id is a permanent compromise. Rotate and bound lifetimes.

items.prompt: Scenario: an internal tool is iframed by an external page and admins' clicks trigger actions. Diagnosis and fix?
items.answer: Clickjacking; send X-Frame-Options: DENY/SAMEORIGIN or CSP frame-ancestors.
items.explain: UI redressing needs framing; framing headers remove the primitive.

items.prompt: Scenario: the app reflects a database error showing table names to users after a malformed input. Two problems?
items.answer: Possible injection probe succeeding, and information disclosure — use parameters and generic user-facing errors.
items.explain: Errors teach attackers the schema. Log specifics server-side; show users nothing useful to an attacker.

handsOnLab.title: Find-and-fix in OWASP Juice Shop
handsOnLab.brief: Run OWASP Juice Shop locally in Docker, reproduce one SQL injection, one reflected XSS, and one stored XSS challenge, then write up the root cause and the correct fix for each as if filing findings for a development team.
steps: Install Docker Desktop (free) for your OS and verify with: docker --version and docker run hello-world.
Pull and run Juice Shop: docker run -d -p 3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop — wait ~30 seconds, then open http://localhost:3000 and dismiss the welcome banner.
Open the Score Board (it lists challenges by category) and filter to Injection and XSS; pick one SQL injection login-bypass challenge.
Reproduce the SQLi: on the login form, enter ' OR 1=1-- in the email field (any password) and observe the admin login. Record the exact payload.
Write the root cause: string-concatenated query. Write the fix: parameterized query — include a 5-line before/after code sketch in your language of choice.
Pick a reflected XSS challenge (e.g., the search field): enter <iframe src="javascript:alert('xss')"> or the challenge's expected payload and confirm execution.
Pick a stored XSS challenge (e.g., a product review/comment): submit a payload, reload, and confirm it fires for the page itself.
For each XSS, write root cause (unencoded output into HTML sink / innerHTML sink) and fix (contextual output encoding; textContent for DOM sinks; CSP as defense-in-depth).
Check the app's response headers with curl -sI http://localhost:3000 and note which security headers are missing.
Draft your find-and-fix report: three findings, each with reproduction steps, root cause, fix, and a one-line regression test idea.
Stop the container: docker stop <container-id> (get it from docker ps).
Re-read your report and confirm every fix you propose eliminates the class, not just the one payload (e.g., parameters, not quote-blocking).
handsOnLab.deliverable: juice-shop-find-and-fix.md — three findings (SQLi, reflected XSS, stored XSS) with reproduction, root cause, class-level fix, and regression test.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: You can log in as admin via the SQLi payload, trigger both XSS payloads, and your report's fixes use parameterized queries and contextual output encoding — not blacklists.

choices: Attacker input was rendered unencoded into ticket pages, so every viewer executed it; verify the output-encoding fix, purge stored payloads, rotate exposed sessions, add CSP and regression tests

notes.title: Network attacker models: from sniffer to on-path adversary
notes.body:
Security reasoning starts by stating what the attacker can do. Network attackers come in three strengths.

The passive eavesdropper can only observe traffic — think open Wi-Fi or a compromised switch mirror port. Against unencrypted HTTP, this attacker reads everything: credentials, session cookies, page contents. Encryption defeats this attacker completely, which is why HTTPS-everywhere was the first big win.

The off-path attacker cannot see your traffic but can send packets that appear to come from someone else — blind spoofing. Classic example: guessing TCP sequence numbers to inject a RST and kill a connection, or sending forged DNS replies hoping to win a race against the real server. Off-path attackers exploit protocols that authenticate weakly or not at all.

The on-path (man-in-the-middle) attacker sits between you and the destination: a rogue access point, a compromised router, ARP spoofing on the LAN. This attacker can observe, block, and modify traffic at will. Only authenticated, integrity-protected encryption (TLS done right) stops this one — and even then, only if you actually verify the certificate instead of clicking through warnings.

The strongest formal model, Dolev-Yao, assumes the attacker controls the entire network: they can intercept, replay, forge, and delay any message, and the only things they cannot do are break cryptography and guess high-entropy secrets. TLS is designed against this adversary. Operator takeaway: when someone says 'the network is trusted,' ask which attacker model that assumes — on most real networks (coffee shops, hotels, shared office LANs), assume on-path capability and encrypt plus authenticate everything. This is also the philosophical root of zero trust: the LAN is not a trust boundary.

Two extensions of the attacker-model idea pay daily dividends. First, the insider and the supply chain: Dolev-Yao assumes the network is hostile, but your threat model should also ask what happens when the endpoint or the vendor is hostile — a compromised update server or a malicious dependency bypasses every network control you built. That's why allowlisting (deny-by-default execution) and reproducible builds matter: they move trust from 'the network delivered it' to 'this exact byte sequence is authorized.' Second, calibrate paranoia to the asset: the same engineer should demand Dolev-Yao-grade protection for credential transport and accept weaker assumptions for public marketing content. Threat modeling isn't about fearing everything equally — it's about spending your strongest controls where the attacker models are strongest and the assets most valuable. Write the assumed attacker at the top of every design doc; when the assumption changes (new network, new integration), the controls get re-examined.

notes.title: ARP spoofing and DNS spoofing: trust without authentication
notes.body:
ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on a local network, and it has no authentication whatsoever: hosts believe the most recent answer they hear. In ARP spoofing, the attacker sends forged ARP replies claiming 'I am the gateway' (binding the gateway's IP to the attacker's MAC). Victims update their ARP caches, and their traffic flows through the attacker, who forwards it onward — a silent man-in-the-middle on the LAN. Worked conceptually: victim V asks 'who has 192.168.1.1 (gateway)?' The attacker A answers first and repeatedly: '192.168.1.1 is at AA:AA:AA (my MAC).' V's cache now points at A. Every packet V sends to the internet goes to A first. Defenses: dynamic ARP inspection on managed switches (the switch validates ARP against its DHCP snooping table), static ARP entries for critical hosts (brittle), and network segmentation so one compromised host can't reach crown-jewel VLANs.

DNS spoofing exploits the same pattern one layer up: classic DNS responses are unauthenticated UDP, so an off-path attacker can race forged answers ('bank.example is at attacker-IP') into a resolver's cache — cache poisoning. The famous Kaminsky-era technique made the race practical by forcing the resolver to query attacker-influenced names, multiplying the attacker's chances. Defenses: DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records so resolvers can verify authenticity (deployment is partial, so know it as the principled fix); DNS over HTTPS/TLS (DoH/DoT) encrypts the stub-to-resolver leg, defeating local sniffing and tampering but moving trust to the resolver operator; and source-port and transaction-ID randomization raised the bar for blind forgery.

The pattern to internalize: any protocol that acts on unauthenticated claims is spoofable. Your job as an operator is to notice which of your protocols those are — ARP, classic DNS, unauthenticated NTP, LLMNR/mDNS name resolution on Windows networks — and either replace, authenticate, or segment them.

On Windows networks, add LLMNR and mDNS/NBNS to your unauthenticated-protocol watchlist. When a hostname doesn't resolve via DNS, Windows helpfully broadcasts 'who is this?' to the local network — and any host may answer. Attackers run responders that answer every such query, harvesting the NTLM authentication attempts victims then send to the attacker's machine (which can be relayed or cracked offline). The mitigations are configuration, not products: disable LLMNR via Group Policy, disable NetBIOS where possible, and enforce SMB signing so relayed authentication can't be weaponized. The pattern is identical to ARP and DNS — unauthenticated local claims believed by default. Your LAN hardening checklist therefore reads: DHCP snooping + dynamic ARP inspection on switches, DNSSEC/DoH where deployable, LLMNR/NBNS disabled via GPO, and segmentation so a compromised workstation can't broadcast-lie to the server VLAN. Every item on that list exists because some protocol trusted the network.

notes.title: Why encryption alone is not enough
notes.body:
A common misconception: 'we encrypt, therefore we're secure.' Encryption without authentication just gives the attacker a private channel to you instead of to the real server.

Worked attack: SSL stripping. You type bank.example into the address bar; the browser first tries http://bank.example. The on-path attacker intercepts that plaintext HTTP request and opens their own HTTPS session to the real bank. You see a page that looks exactly like the bank (served by the attacker over plain HTTP or over HTTPS with the attacker's own valid certificate for a lookalike domain), you log in, and the attacker relays everything to the real bank over real TLS. Your traffic was 'encrypted' — to the wrong party. The defense is authentication before trust: verify you are talking to the real bank via its certificate, and never downgrade: HSTS (next notes) tells browsers to refuse plaintext for a domain, killing the stripping primitive.

Three properties a secure channel needs, and encryption provides only one: confidentiality (no one else reads it) — encryption handles this. Authentication (you are talking to the intended party) — certificates and signatures handle this. Integrity (messages aren't modified in transit) — message authentication codes / AEAD handle this. TLS provides all three, but only if the handshake's authentication step is honored: every 'click through this certificate warning' trains users and operators to discard the authentication property while keeping the padlock-shaped placebo. Operator rule: a certificate error is the protocol screaming that the authentication step failed. The correct response is to stop and investigate, never to bypass — bypassing converts TLS into encryption-to-attacker.

The authentication gap appears inside cryptography too, which is why authenticated encryption (AEAD) replaced the old encrypt-then-MAC-by-hand era. Cipher modes like GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 bind confidentiality and integrity into one construction — you can't accidentally encrypt without authenticating, because the API won't let you. Similarly, Diffie-Hellman alone is anonymous: two parties can agree on a secret while a middle person agrees separately with each (the classic DH MitM). TLS fixes this by signing the DH exchange with the server's certificate key — authentication of the key exchange, not just of a later message. And downgrade attacks generalize beyond SSL stripping: any negotiation (protocol version, cipher suite) that an attacker can edit in flight is a downgrade surface, which is why TLS 1.3 signs the entire transcript in Finished and removed the weak options rather than merely deprecating them. The design principle: never negotiate security properties over an unauthenticated channel without integrity-protecting the negotiation itself.

notes.title: The TLS handshake: what each step proves
notes.body:
The TLS handshake's job: turn an untrusted network into an authenticated, confidential, integrity-protected channel, with forward secrecy. Here is the TLS 1.3 shape (1.2 is similar but with more round trips and negotiable, weaker options — one reason 1.3 removed them).

Step 1 — ClientHello: the client sends supported versions, cipher suites, and a key share (an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman public value). Proves nothing yet; it is an offer. The key share is the forward-secrecy seed: because it is ephemeral (generated fresh per connection and discarded after), a future key compromise cannot decrypt today's traffic.

Step 2 — ServerHello: the server picks the version and cipher, sends its own ephemeral key share. Now both sides can compute the same shared secret without ever transmitting it — that is the Diffie-Hellman trick: each combines its private value with the other's public value. An eavesdropper seeing both public values cannot compute the secret.

Step 3 — Certificate + CertificateVerify: the server sends its certificate chain (leaf for its domain, signed by intermediates up to a root the client trusts) and a digital signature over the handshake transcript made with the private key matching the leaf certificate. This is the authentication step: only the true holder of the private key could produce that signature, and the chain ties the key to the domain name via trusted CAs. This defeats the on-path attacker — they cannot forge the signature.

Step 4 — Finished: both sides send a message authentication code over the entire handshake transcript, keyed with the new session keys. This proves no one tampered with the negotiation itself (it defeats downgrade attacks that try to edit the ClientHello in flight — any edit breaks the Finished verification).

Then application data flows under AEAD encryption (confidentiality + integrity per record). Session resumption (PSK/tickets) trades a bit of forward secrecy for speed on reconnects — fine for most uses, worth knowing exists.

Worked verification you can do today: openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -tls1_3 shows the negotiated version and cipher; -showcerts dumps the chain. If the handshake completes with a valid chain, you have all three properties against a Dolev-Yao network attacker. If any step is skipped or bypassed, name which property you lost.

Know how TLS 1.3 differs from 1.2, because you'll meet both. TLS 1.2 negotiates in two round trips, supports RSA key transport (the client encrypts a secret to the server's public key — no forward secrecy, since a later key compromise decrypts everything), and offers cipher suites including weak ones (RC4, 3DES, CBC modes with their padding oracles) that misconfiguration can select. TLS 1.3 does the handshake in one round trip (the client guesses the key share up front), removed RSA key transport and static DH entirely (forward secrecy is mandatory, not optional), cut the cipher suite list to five strong AEAD options, and encrypted more of the handshake itself (reducing metadata leakage). Migration reality: you'll support 1.2 for legacy clients for years — so your server configuration must explicitly disable the weak 1.2 options rather than relying on 1.3's cleanliness. Test with openssl s_client using -tls1_2 plus specific -cipher flags to confirm the weak ones actually refuse.

notes.title: Certificate chains and trust: how authentication actually works
notes.body:
A certificate binds a public key to an identity ('this key belongs to bank.example') via a trusted third party's signature. Trust is chained: the leaf certificate (the server's) is signed by an intermediate CA, which is signed by a root CA whose certificate ships in your OS/browser trust store. Validation is the client walking this chain and checking every link.

The validation checklist, in order: (1) Signatures: each certificate's signature verifies with the issuer's public key, up the chain to a trusted root. One bad signature = reject. (2) Name matching: the domain you're visiting must appear in the leaf's Subject Alternative Names (SANs). A valid cert for evil.example does not authenticate bank.example — this is why phishing sites with real certificates for their own lookalike domains still don't pass as the bank. (3) Validity period: the current time must fall between notBefore and notAfter. Expired cert = reject; this bounds the damage of a compromised key. (4) Revocation: has this certificate been revoked since issuance? Checked via CRLs (lists) or OCSP (per-cert queries), with OCSP stapling letting the server provide a fresh OCSP response itself. Revocation checking is the ecosystem's weakest link in practice — soft-fail behaviors mean a blocked OCSP responder often results in 'proceed anyway.'

Certificate types (domain-validated, organization-validated, extended-validation) differ in how much identity vetting the CA did before issuance. For your threat model, what matters is: DV proves control of the domain at issuance time — enough to stop network attackers, not enough to prove the business behind the domain is legitimate.

Operator gotchas: private PKI (corporate roots pushed to managed devices) is normal inside enterprises — don't confuse an enterprise TLS-inspection root with an attack, but do verify it came from your IT; wildcard certs (*.example.com) are convenient and increase blast radius if the key leaks; and certificate transparency logs mean every public cert is publicly logged — you can monitor them for certs issued for your domains that you didn't request.

Enterprises run private PKI, and you should know what normal looks like: the company pushes its own root certificate to managed devices so the TLS-inspecting proxy (or internal services) chains to it. On a managed laptop, seeing an unfamiliar root is expected; on your personal device, the same root is a red flag — context decides, and verifying the root's provenance with IT is the correct response either way. For your public domains, use Certificate Transparency monitoring: every publicly trusted cert is logged to public CT logs, so you can watch for certificates issued for your domains that you didn't request — the early warning for mis-issuance or attacker-provisioned certs. Several free monitors do this; set one up for every domain you own. And revisit wildcards with fresh eyes: a wildcard's convenience is real for fleets of subdomains, but scope the risk deliberately — if the wildcard key lives on 200 servers, your blast radius is 200 servers, and per-service certificates with automation (ACME-style issuance and renewal) are the modern answer to the management burden wildcards were papering over.

notes.title: HTTPS pitfalls: mixed content, missing HSTS, and warning fatigue
notes.body:
TLS done right still fails if the surrounding deployment is sloppy. The big three pitfalls:

Mixed content: an HTTPS page that loads subresources over HTTP. Active mixed content (scripts, iframes, XHR) is catastrophic — an on-path attacker replaces the HTTP-loaded script with their own, and it executes in the HTTPS page's origin with full privileges. Browsers block active mixed content by default now. Passive mixed content (images, video) 'only' leaks cookies and page-view privacy and enables image replacement; browsers warn but historically allowed it. The fix is trivial and absolute: serve everything over HTTPS, then set Content-Security-Policy: upgrade-insecure-requests as a backstop during migration.

Missing HSTS: without Strict-Transport-Security, the first visit to a site (or any visit after the browser forgets) starts as plaintext HTTP, which is exactly the window SSL stripping exploits. HSTS is a response header (Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains) telling the browser 'for the next year, refuse to use HTTP for this domain — upgrade automatically and treat cert errors as hard failures.' HSTS preloading (browsers shipping a baked-in list) closes even the first-visit window. Rollout order matters: deploy HTTPS everywhere first, then a short max-age, then long, then preload — a premature includeSubDomains can brick plaintext-only subdomains.

Warning fatigue and click-through: every bypassed cert warning teaches the human to ignore the authentication step. As an operator, treat user cert-warning bypasses as a training and tooling problem: investigate the underlying cause (expired cert, captive portal, inspection root missing) rather than normalizing the click-through.

Audit routine for any site you own: fetch the headers (curl -sI), confirm HSTS with long max-age and includeSubDomains, confirm no active mixed content (browser devtools console flags it), confirm the cert chain validates with full chain served (missing intermediates are the most common server misconfiguration), and confirm weak protocols are off — negotiate with openssl using -tls1, -tls1_1 flags and expect failure.

HSTS deployment has a careful rollout order because the header is a loaded gun: it tells browsers to refuse plaintext, period. Deploy HTTPS everywhere first and verify no plaintext-only subdomains remain (includeSubDomains will brick them). Then set a short max-age (a day), watch for breakage, extend to a year, and only then consider HSTS preloading — submitting your domain to the browser preload list, which closes even the first-visit window but is deliberately hard to reverse (removal takes months to propagate). On certificate errors and users: the operational fix for warning fatigue is making the legitimate cases painless — captive portals should be detected and explained, inspection roots should deploy silently via device management, and expirations should never reach users because monitoring caught them. Every warning a user sees should be rare enough to take seriously. And on revocation's soft-fail problem: know that browsers often 'fail open' when OCSP responders are unreachable (availability beats security in their trade-off), which is why short-lived certificates are gaining favor — expiry becomes the revocation mechanism, no responder needed.

notes.title: From TLS to endpoint Network Control
notes.body:
TLS protects data in transit between endpoints. ThreatLocker's Network Control protects the endpoints themselves: an endpoint firewall with dynamic ACLs that open and close ports, blocking lateral movement and command-and-control even when traffic is encrypted. The two compose: TLS stops the network attacker; Network Control stops the compromised endpoint from becoming the network attacker.

Why both matter: TLS cannot see inside encrypted tunnels — neither can your IDS, which is exactly why attackers exfiltrate over HTTPS and DNS. An allowlisted endpoint that may only talk to its update server and its SaaS apps over defined ports has no room for a C2 channel regardless of encryption. Conversely, a perfect firewall policy with plaintext protocols still leaks to the passive sniffer. Defense in depth means the properties compose: confidentiality+integrity+authentication on the wire (TLS), least-privilege connectivity at the host (Network Control), least-privilege execution on the host (Allowlisting + Ringfencing).

Operator scenarios to rehearse: (1) A server's certificate expires at 2 AM — your monitoring should catch it before users do; check expiry in your TLS audit. (2) Malware on a workstation beacons over HTTPS to a fresh domain — TLS hides the payload, but Network Control's deny-by-default egress and Detect's IOC alerts catch the behavior. (3) A user on hotel Wi-Fi hits a captive portal with a cert warning — train the response: portals legitimately break TLS; log in, then verify the warning clears before doing anything sensitive. The through-line of this module: name the attacker model, name which property each control provides, and never assume one control covers another's job.

Map threats to controls explicitly and the architecture sells itself. Passive sniffer → TLS everywhere (M18). On-path active attacker → TLS with real certificate validation plus HSTS (M18). Malicious or compromised code on the endpoint → Allowlisting: it never runs (ThreatLocker Application Control). Trusted app turned against you (Word spawning PowerShell) → Ringfencing: the app can't reach outside its role. Stolen credentials used at 2 AM → authentication controls (M20) plus behavioral detection (M23). Data sneaking out over HTTPS → Storage Control and Network Control constraining exfiltration paths, Detect raising the alarm. No single control covers two rows — that's the point of the table, and it's your answer when anyone asks 'why do we need all of these?' In the interview, walk the panel through one scenario across the whole stack; operators who think in layers, naming which property each layer provides and which attacker it stops, are exactly who ThreatLocker hires.

cards.front: Three network attacker strengths, weakest to strongest?
cards.back: Passive eavesdropper (observe only), off-path (spoof blindly), on-path/MitM (observe, block, modify).

cards.front: What is the Dolev-Yao attacker model?
cards.back: Attacker controls the whole network — intercept, replay, forge, delay anything — but cannot break crypto or guess high-entropy secrets.

cards.front: How does ARP spoofing work, in one line?
cards.back: Attacker sends forged unauthenticated ARP replies binding the gateway's IP to their MAC; victims' traffic flows through the attacker.

cards.front: Why is classic DNS spoofable, and what are two mitigations?
cards.back: Responses are unauthenticated UDP — forgeable by racing. Mitigations: DNSSEC (signed records) and DoH/DoT (encrypted transport).

cards.front: What three properties must a secure channel provide?
cards.back: Confidentiality, authentication, integrity. Encryption alone gives only the first.

cards.front: What does the TLS CertificateVerify step prove?
cards.back: The server holds the private key matching the leaf certificate — it authenticates the server to the client.

cards.front: What does the TLS Finished message prove?
cards.back: Handshake integrity — neither side's negotiation messages were tampered with (defeats downgrade attacks).

cards.front: What gives TLS forward secrecy?
cards.back: Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key shares, generated fresh per connection and discarded after.

cards.front: Four certificate validation checks, in order?
cards.back: Signature chain to a trusted root, SAN name match, validity period, revocation status.

cards.front: Active vs passive mixed content?
cards.back: Active (scripts/iframes): attacker-replaceable code — browsers block. Passive (images): privacy leak — warn. Fix: HTTPS everywhere.

cards.front: What does HSTS do, and what attack does it kill?
cards.back: Forces HTTPS-only for a domain (upgrades HTTP, hard-fails cert errors); kills SSL-stripping downgrade attacks.

cards.front: Correct operator response to a certificate warning?
cards.back: Stop and investigate — never click through. Bypassing discards TLS's authentication property.

quiz.q: An attacker on open Wi-Fi only captures packets. Which attacker is this, and what defeats them?
quiz.explain: Passive observation is defeated by confidentiality alone — properly configured TLS makes captured traffic unreadable. No authentication bypass is needed for this attacker.

quiz.q: In ARP spoofing, what exactly does the attacker forge?
choices: ARP replies binding the gateway's IP to the attacker's MAC
DNS responses for the victim's queries
DHCP leases for the whole subnet
quiz.explain: ARP has no authentication, so the most recent claim wins. Poisoning the victim's ARP cache redirects their traffic through the attacker, who forwards it on.

quiz.q: You type bank.example; the browser first tries HTTP and an on-path attacker relays you to the real bank while reading everything. This is…
choices: SSL stripping — defeated by HSTS and never downgrading
ARP spoofing — defeated by static ARP
Session fixation — defeated by id rotation
quiz.explain: The attacker exploits the plaintext first hop to become the TLS endpoint on both sides. HSTS removes the plaintext window; the authentication step only works if you don't bypass it.

quiz.q: In the TLS 1.3 handshake, what is the purpose of the ephemeral key shares in Hello messages?
choices: Forward secrecy — per-connection secrets discarded after use
quiz.explain: Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman means each connection's keys are fresh and destroyed afterward, so a later key compromise can't decrypt recorded traffic.

quiz.q: A server presents a valid, trusted certificate for evil-example.com while you meant to visit bank.example. What happens?
choices: Validation fails on SAN name matching — the cert doesn't name bank.example
Validation succeeds because the chain is trusted
The Finished message fixes the mismatch
quiz.explain: Chain trust is necessary but not sufficient — the leaf must name the domain you asked for. Phishing certs for lookalike domains fail exactly here.

quiz.q: An HTTPS page loads its analytics script over HTTP. Why is this critical?
choices: Active mixed content — an on-path attacker can replace the script and run code in the page's origin
It only leaks the page title
quiz.explain: Scripts are active content: substituted script executes with the HTTPS origin's privileges — equivalent to XSS delivered by the network. Browsers block it; the fix is HTTPS everywhere.

quiz.q: OCSP stapling solves which problem?
choices: Lets the server provide a fresh revocation status itself, avoiding a separate client OCSP fetch
quiz.explain: Revocation checks are slow and privacy-leaking when clients fetch them; stapling has the server attach a recent OCSP response to the handshake.

quiz.q: Why is a wildcard certificate (*.example.com) a larger risk than a single-name cert if its key leaks?
choices: One key authenticates every subdomain — larger blast radius
quiz.explain: Compromise scope follows the names on the cert. Convenience (one cert for many hosts) trades against blast radius — a standard risk decision.

quiz.q: TLS hides malware's HTTPS beacon from IDS. Which endpoint control addresses this, and how?
choices: Network Control — deny-by-default egress and dynamic ACLs block unauthorized connections regardless of encryption
Certificate pinning — it drops the beacon
quiz.explain: Encryption blinds network inspection, so the control point moves to the endpoint: only allowlisted destinations and ports may be reached, and Detect raises IOC alerts on the behavior.

quiz.q: openssl s_client -connect site:443 -tls1 fails but -tls1_2 succeeds. What does this tell you?
choices: The server correctly refuses the obsolete TLS 1.0 — good hygiene
quiz.explain: Probing with old protocol flags is how you audit TLS hygiene: refusal of TLS 1.0/1.1 is the desired outcome. Old versions have known weaknesses and should be disabled.

items.prompt: Name the three attacker strengths in order.
items.answer: Passive eavesdropper, off-path, on-path (MitM).
items.explain: Each stronger attacker defeats more defenses; design for on-path.

items.prompt: What assumption does Dolev-Yao make about the network?
items.answer: The attacker fully controls it — intercept, replay, forge, delay — but can't break crypto.
items.explain: TLS is designed against this adversary; that's the bar.

items.prompt: One-line: why is ARP spoofable?
items.answer: ARP replies are unauthenticated; hosts trust the latest claim.
items.explain: No-authentication protocols are spoofable — the recurring pattern.

items.prompt: Three properties of a secure channel?
items.answer: Confidentiality, authentication, integrity.
items.explain: Encryption alone gives only confidentiality.

items.prompt: Which handshake step authenticates the server?
items.answer: Certificate + CertificateVerify (signature with the leaf's private key).
items.explain: Only the true key holder can sign the transcript.

items.prompt: Which handshake step guarantees no downgrade tampering?
items.answer: Finished — MAC over the full handshake transcript.
items.explain: Any in-flight edit breaks Finished verification.

items.prompt: What does HSTS force, and what does it defeat?
items.answer: HTTPS-only for the domain; defeats SSL-stripping downgrades.
items.explain: Removes the plaintext first-hop window.

items.prompt: Scenario: users report cert warnings only on the guest Wi-Fi, and the warning clears after portal login. Diagnosis?
items.answer: Captive portal intercepting TLS pre-auth; expected. Train: log in, then confirm warnings clear before sensitive use.
items.explain: Portals must break TLS to redirect — the warning is the protocol working as designed.

items.prompt: Scenario: openssl shows the server sends only the leaf cert, no intermediates, and some clients fail. Fix?
items.answer: Serve the full chain including intermediates; clients lacking them can't build trust.
items.explain: Missing intermediates is the most common TLS server misconfiguration.

items.prompt: Scenario: a phishing site has a valid DV cert for bank-secure-login.com. Does TLS protect the victim?
items.answer: TLS protects the connection to the attacker's domain; it does not prove the site is the real bank. SAN matching + user vigilance matter.
items.explain: DV certs prove domain control, not legitimacy. Authentication is to the named identity — check the name.

items.prompt: Scenario: you need to confirm a server rejects TLS 1.0. Exact probe?
items.answer: openssl s_client -connect host:443 -tls1 and expect handshake failure.
items.explain: Negative testing with old-protocol flags audits hygiene directly.

items.prompt: Scenario: malware beacons over HTTPS; the NIDS sees only encrypted flows. Which controls catch it?
items.answer: Endpoint Network Control (deny-by-default egress, dynamic ACLs) plus Detect IOC alerts on the behavior.
items.explain: When encryption blinds the network, the control point moves to the endpoint.

items.prompt: Scenario: cert expires in 6 hours on a production site. What's the blast radius and the process fix?
items.answer: All clients hard-fail closed (or warn); fix process: expiry monitoring with alerts well before renewal deadlines, automation.
items.explain: Expiry is the most embarrassing outage — it's fully predictable, so monitor it.

handsOnLab.title: TLS inspection and HTTPS hygiene audit
handsOnLab.brief: Use openssl and curl to inspect the live TLS configuration of three real sites, evaluate their certificate chains, protocol versions, and HSTS posture, and write an audit report with findings and remediation advice.
steps: Verify openssl exists: openssl version. (Windows: use Git Bash or WSL; macOS/Linux have it.)
Pick three sites: one bank or major SaaS, one site you suspect is sloppy (a small local business), and interstitiumlabs.dev.
For each: run openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST -tls1_3 < /dev/null and record the negotiated protocol and cipher suite.
Re-run with -showcerts; paste the chain into your notes and count: leaf, intermediate(s), root. Note whether intermediates are served.
Check expiry: echo | openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -subject -issuer.
Negative-test old protocols: try -tls1 and -tls1_1 against each host; record whether the handshake fails (good) or succeeds (finding).
Fetch headers: curl -sI https://HOST | grep -i strict and record max-age, includeSubDomains, preload presence.
Check for mixed content: load each site in a browser, open devtools console, and note any mixed-content warnings.
Write tls-audit.md: per site — chain summary, protocol/cipher, expiry date, HSTS status, mixed-content status, old-protocol results.
For each finding, write the remediation in one line (e.g., 'serve intermediates', 'add HSTS includeSubDomains', 'disable TLS 1.0/1.1').
Rank the three sites best to worst with a one-sentence justification each.
Re-read your chain notes and confirm you can state what each handshake step proved for one site.
handsOnLab.deliverable: tls-audit.md — three-site audit with chain, protocol, expiry, HSTS, mixed-content, and remediation per finding.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: You can point at each site's chain and name leaf/intermediate/root, state which old protocols were refused, and quote each site's HSTS max-age.
