choices: Treat the session as potentially compromised: force password reset and session invalidation, investigate whether it was a captive portal or interception, and retrain on never bypassing cert warnings
Tell them warnings on hotel Wi-Fi are always safe to ignore
Block hotel networks at the firewall
mockTask.explain: A bypassed cert warning means the TLS authentication step was discarded — the session may have been proxied. Contain (reset credentials, kill sessions), investigate the cause (portal vs attacker), and fix the human factor: bypassing is never the procedure.

title: MIT 6.858: Side-Channel Attacks & Defenses
summary: Secrets leak through physical behavior — time, cache, power. Learn timing attacks with a worked byte-by-byte recovery, cache and power analysis concepts, and the defenses that matter: constant-time code, blinding, and noise. Includes a hands-on timing experiment in Python.
objectives: Explain the side-channel concept: secrets leaking through timing, cache, power, or EM behavior rather than protocol flaws.
Walk through a timing attack recovering a secret token byte by byte using an early-exit comparison.
Describe cache-timing and power-analysis attacks at the concept level and what each requires of the attacker.
Write constant-time comparison code and explain why it defeats timing attacks.
Name layered defenses — blinding, masking, noise, rate limiting — and when each applies.

notes.title: The core idea: the implementation leaks what the math hides
notes.body:
Cryptography proves things about algorithms: 'recovering this key requires 2^128 operations.' Side-channel attacks ignore the algorithm and watch the implementation's physical behavior — how long it takes, how much power it draws, which cache lines it touches, even the sound it makes. The math is unbroken; the machine running it is chatty.

The attacker model: the adversary can observe some physical side channel while the victim performs a secret-dependent operation. Sometimes that observation is remote — measuring response times over a network. Sometimes it needs proximity — a probe on a smart card's power line, or co-residency on shared cloud hardware for cache attacks. The common thread is that secret data influences observable behavior: a branch taken only when a key bit is 1, a memory access pattern that depends on the plaintext, a multiplication that draws measurably more power for certain operands.

A concrete everyday example: a web login that compares the submitted password hash to the stored hash with a loop that returns False at the first mismatched byte. The response time grows with the number of correct leading bytes. That timing difference is the side channel, and it converts an unguessable 256-bit token into 32 independent 8-bit guessing problems — each solvable by trying all 256 values and picking the slowest. The fix costs one line (compare everything, then decide), but the vulnerability pattern recurs everywhere developers write 'clever' early exits.

Why this matters to you as an operator even if you never write crypto: you will review code, choose libraries, and configure systems. Knowing that variable-time comparison is a vulnerability — not an optimization — changes how you read authentication code, token validation, and HMAC checks for the rest of your career. And when you evaluate a crypto library, 'constant-time implementation' is one of the first properties you check.

Scope the attacker model before you worry: remote timing over the internet needs thousands of samples and a measurable signal — it threatens authentication oracles and token endpoints, not your laptop's disk encryption. Co-resident cache attacks need shared hardware — they threaten multi-tenant cloud and shared CI, not your home PC. Power and EM analysis need physical possession — they threaten smart cards, phones, and unattended devices, not servers in locked racks. This scoping is the 6.858 habit applied: name the observer's position and capabilities, then ask which of your secrets are exposed to that position. Two more exotic channels to know exist: acoustic eavesdropping (research has recovered keystrokes and even RSA keys from the sounds of keyboards and electronics — microphones are sensors too), and electromagnetic emanations (the basis of TEMPEST-style attacks on displays and cables). You won't defend against these daily, but knowing the channel space exists keeps you from declaring anything 'physically impossible' prematurely.

notes.title: Timing attacks: recovering a token byte by byte
notes.body:
The classic timing attack exploits early-exit comparison. Here is the vulnerable pattern:

def insecure_compare(a, b):
    if len(a) != len(b): return False
    for x, y in zip(a, b):
        if x != y: return False   # early exit: leaks position of first mismatch
    return True

Worked attack: the server checks a 16-byte API token with this function and returns 200/401. You, the attacker, control the candidate token and can measure response times. For byte position 0, you try all 256 values. 255 of them mismatch at position 0 and return fast; one matches position 0, proceeds to position 1, and returns slightly slower. The slowest candidate is the correct first byte. Repeat for position 1 (now the timing gap appears at the second byte), and so on. After 16 x 256 = 4096 requests, you hold the full token — versus 256^16 guesses by brute force.

Over a network, one timing sample is noisy — jitter from routers, load, and scheduling dwarfs a nanosecond-scale difference. Attackers compensate with statistics: thousands of samples per candidate, medians instead of means, and attacking the coarsest signal first (e.g., distinguishing 'mismatch at byte 0' from 'mismatch at byte 5' is easier than byte 14 vs 15 because the gap accumulates). Real remote timing attacks have been demonstrated against web applications and even against TLS implementations (Lucky 13 against CBC-mode TLS exploited tiny timing differences in padding validation, amplified over many connections).

Defenses at the code level: compare in constant time — always examine every byte, accumulate differences with bitwise OR, and decide once at the end (Python's hmac.compare_digest does exactly this; use it for every secret comparison). At the system level: rate-limit authentication attempts (4096 rapid probes should trip alarms, not succeed), add random delays (raises attacker cost but is not a complete fix — statistics still win eventually), and prefer designs where the attacker can't get a timing oracle at all (e.g., don't reveal whether the username or the password was wrong — though usability debates continue).

The Lucky 13 attack is the canonical real-world remote timing attack and worth knowing by name: it targeted TLS's CBC-mode padding validation, where the server's error handling took measurably different time depending on whether padding was valid. Over many connections, attackers amplified the tiny timing difference statistically and decrypted traffic byte by byte — against real servers, over real networks. The industry's response was to move to AEAD cipher suites (TLS 1.3 removed CBC entirely), which is why your M18 knowledge and this module connect: protocol design must eliminate the oracle, not just shrink it. A cousin lives in web apps: blind SQL injection via timing (IF(1=1, SLEEP(5), 0)) turns the database into a timing oracle for exfiltrating data one bit per request — same statistics, same defense principle (parameterize so the oracle never exists). And on measurement: attackers use medians over thousands of samples and attack the coarsest signal first; your lab's jump from 200 to 5000 trials with jitter demonstrates exactly why 'we added a random delay' is not a fix.

notes.title: Cache attacks: when shared hardware betrays you
notes.body:
Modern CPUs share cache between processes, cores, and even virtual machines on the same host. Cache attacks exploit a simple physical fact: accessing data already in cache is fast; accessing data that must be fetched from RAM is slow. By measuring their own memory access times, attackers infer what the victim touched.

The canonical technique is Flush+Reload, conceptually: (1) the attacker flushes a shared memory line from the cache (using an instruction like clflush, or by evicting it); (2) the attacker waits while the victim runs; (3) the attacker reloads the same line and times it. Fast reload = the victim accessed that line (it got pulled back into cache). Slow reload = the victim didn't. This works when attacker and victim share memory pages — common with shared libraries and kernel same-page merging in virtualized environments.

What does this buy? Demonstrated research has recovered AES keys from co-resident VMs by watching cache access patterns during encryption (table lookups indexed by key-dependent values touch different cache lines), detected keystrokes by watching cache lines in shared UI libraries, and fingerprinted browsing activity. The requirements are real but nontrivial: shared hardware or memory, the ability to run code alongside the victim, and high-resolution timers — which is why these attacks matter most for cloud multi-tenancy, shared CI runners, and browser JavaScript (where timers were deliberately coarsened as a mitigation after Spectre/Meltdown).

Defenses: constant-time, cache-oblivious algorithms (AES-NI hardware instructions don't do key-dependent table lookups — prefer hardware crypto); cache partitioning or disabling sharing (hypervisors can disable page merging); and reducing timer resolution available to untrusted code. Operator relevance: when you place sensitive crypto workloads, know your tenancy — dedicated hosts exist partly because shared silicon is a side channel.

Spectre and Meltdown are cache side channels wearing a speculation costume, and understanding that reframes them: speculative execution makes the CPU touch secret-dependent memory, the cache remembers what was touched, and Flush+Reload-style timing reads the cache out. The speculation is just the delivery mechanism; the exfiltration is the cache timing channel from this note. That's why the mitigations split the same way: microcode and software barriers to limit speculation's reach, and the longer-term push toward hardware that doesn't leave secret-dependent cache footprints. For browsers, the response included coarsening timer resolution (performance.now() got fuzzier) and site isolation — because high-resolution timers plus shared processes had turned every web page into a potential cache-attack observer. For your infrastructure: keep hypervisors and firmware patched (side-channel mitigations ship in microcode), disable memory deduplication across trust boundaries, and treat 'noisy neighbor' performance anomalies on shared hosts as worth a glance — you probably won't catch a cache attack in the wild, but the hygiene that blunts them is the same hygiene that hardens everything else.

notes.title: Power and electromagnetic analysis: reading the current
notes.body:
Every transistor switch draws current, so a chip's power consumption is a direct function of the data it's processing. Power analysis attacks measure that current — with a resistor in the supply line, an EM probe near the package, even the device's own battery gauge in some demonstrations — and correlate it with secret data.

Simple power analysis (SPA): one trace, visual inspection. Worked concept: RSA modular exponentiation often uses square-and-multiply — square for every key bit, multiply only when the bit is 1. On a power trace, squares and multiplies have visibly different shapes, so a single trace reads the key bits off like Morse code. The defense is making operations indistinguishable: always square AND multiply (dummy operations), or use algorithms with no key-dependent branches (Montgomery ladder).

Differential power analysis (DPA): many traces plus statistics. The attacker records thousands of power traces while the device encrypts known plaintexts, then guesses one key byte at a time: for each of the 256 guesses, they predict what an intermediate value would be and check which guess's prediction correlates with the measured power. The correct guess correlates; wrong guesses don't. DPA defeats naive dummy-operation defenses because statistics separate signal from noise — the defense must break the correlation itself: masking (split every sensitive value into random shares so no single signal carries the secret) and shuffling (randomize operation order).

Where you meet this: smart cards, hardware security modules, phones doing on-device crypto, and IoT devices an attacker can physically hold. You will likely never run a DPA rig, but you must understand why 'the crypto is AES-256' is not the whole answer when someone proposes a $2 microcontroller for a payment terminal — the implementation's physical behavior is part of the security boundary, and certified hardware exists precisely because getting this right is brutally hard.

Electromagnetic analysis deserves its own mental slot because it's contactless: a near-field probe near the chip package picks up EM emanations correlated with switching activity — no need to cut into the power line. Demonstrations have recovered keys from phones and microcontrollers across small air gaps, which matters for 'attacker briefly near the device' threat models (hotel rooms, border crossings, shared offices). Smartphones add sensor side channels: research has shown motion sensors, power gauges, and even auto-brightness behavior leaking keystrokes or app activity to malicious apps holding innocent-looking permissions. The defense economics are brutal — masking and shielding raise chip cost and design complexity, which is why certified secure elements exist: the certification (Common Criteria and similar schemes) is largely about evidencing exactly these implementation-level defenses. Your practical takeaway stays the same: for high-value keys, use hardware designed and certified for the physical attacker, not a general-purpose chip running a software cipher and hoping nobody brings a probe.

notes.title: Defenses: constant time, blinding, masking, and noise
notes.body:
Side-channel defenses form a layered toolkit. Apply them in order of leverage:

Constant-time code is the foundation for software: no secret-dependent branches, no secret-dependent memory accesses, no early exits. Worked example — the secure comparison:

def secure_compare(a, b):
    if len(a) != len(b): return False
    diff = 0
    for x, y in zip(a, b):
        diff |= x ^ y      # examine EVERY byte, accumulate
    return diff == 0      # single decision at the end

Execution time now depends only on length, not content. Note the subtlety: comparing lengths first is fine (lengths usually aren't secret), but if they were, you'd need to handle that too. Also note what constant-time does NOT fix: it fixes timing, not power or cache — a constant-time table lookup still touches key-dependent cache lines. True constant-time means constant in every observable dimension you care about.

Blinding randomizes the computation so the side channel carries no stable secret: RSA blinding multiplies the ciphertext by a random value before decryption and divides it out after — the power trace now reflects random data, and DPA correlation collapses. Masking splits secrets into random shares processed separately. Both are standard in serious crypto implementations — which is why you use vetted libraries rather than writing your own.

Noise and rate limiting raise attacker cost at the system level: random delays, jitter, and aggressive rate limiting on authentication endpoints turn a 4096-request timing attack into a week-long, alarm-tripping campaign. But treat noise as defense-in-depth, never the primary fix — statistics are patient.

Hardware and platform mitigations: use CPU crypto instructions (AES-NI), HSMs for key operations, disable memory deduplication across trust boundaries, and keep firmware patched — microcode updates have repeatedly shipped side-channel mitigations (Speculative execution attacks like Spectre/Meltdown are, at root, cache side channels fed by speculation). The operator's summary: choose constant-time libraries, compare secrets with constant-time functions, rate-limit oracles, and isolate sensitive crypto from untrusted neighbors.

Two implementation subtleties separate textbook constant-time from real constant-time. First, compilers are adversaries: an optimizing compiler may 'helpfully' transform your carefully branchless code back into branches, or eliminate the 'redundant' operations your masking depends on. Serious crypto code is written with compiler behavior in mind (volatile barriers, verified assembly for hot paths) and tested with tools that check the compiled output, not just the source. Second, RSA blinding's math is worth seeing once: to decrypt ciphertext c with private key, pick random r, compute c' = c · r^e mod n, decrypt c' to get m' = m · r mod n, then divide out r. Every decryption now processes randomized data; DPA correlation against the real key collapses because the power trace reflects r, not m. The randomness must be fresh per operation and the division exact — blinding done sloppily (reused r, biased r) leaks again. The lesson for operators: these defenses are subtle enough that 'we implemented our own' is a red flag and 'we use a vetted library' is the answer you want to hear.

notes.title: Why operators must care: reviewing code and choosing libraries
notes.body:
You may never implement RSA, but side-channel awareness changes three operator decisions:

First, code review. Anywhere your systems compare secrets — API tokens, webhook signatures, password reset tokens, HMACs — verify the comparison is constant-time. In Python that's hmac.compare_digest; in Node it's crypto.timingSafeEqual; in most languages there's an equivalent. Flag every == on secret material you see in review. Also flag 'clever' early exits in auth paths as vulnerabilities, not optimizations. This single habit prevents the most likely timing attack you'll ever encounter: the one against your own application.

Second, library selection. When you need crypto, you choose implementations, and 'constant-time' belongs on your evaluation checklist next to 'maintained' and 'audited.' Prefer platform primitives (OS keychains, HSMs, cloud KMS) that push key operations into hardened environments over handling raw keys in application memory. When a vendor claims side-channel resistance, ask which channels (timing? cache? power?) and against which attacker (remote? co-resident? physical?) — vague claims are marketing.

Third, incident thinking. If an attacker had prolonged, high-volume access to an authentication oracle — thousands of timed requests against a token endpoint — consider that timing data may have been harvested, rotate the secrets, and check whether the comparison was constant-time. Your monitoring should alert on the pattern: sustained, systematic probing of auth endpoints is reconnaissance for this exact attack class.

The through-line from 6.858: the threat model must include the implementation's physical behavior, not just the protocol's logic. The mathematically perfect cipher in a chatty implementation is a locked door with the key under the mat — and your job is to notice the mat.

Build the review habit into a checklist you can run on any codebase in an afternoon. One: grep for secret comparisons — every ==, !=, or early-return comparison involving tokens, HMACs, hashes, or reset codes gets flagged for compare_digest/timingSafeEqual equivalents. Two: check randomness sources — token and key generation must use cryptographic RNGs (secrets module, not random), because a predictable token needs no side channel. Three: look at auth endpoints for rate limiting and anomaly alerting — the oracle is only exploitable if the attacker can sample freely. Four: inventory crypto libraries and confirm they're maintained, vetted implementations with constant-time claims, not hand-rolled or abandoned. Five: for high-value systems, ask about tenancy and physical exposure — shared hosts, devices that leave the building. In the interview, this checklist is gold: 'here's how I'd review authentication code on day one' shows operator judgment, not just trivia. And the monitoring complement: alert on sustained systematic probing of auth endpoints (thousands of similar requests, one IP, growing response-time analysis is hard to see directly — but the request pattern is visible).

cards.front: What is a side-channel attack, in one sentence?
cards.back: Recovering secrets by observing physical behavior (timing, cache, power, EM) of an implementation rather than breaking the algorithm.

cards.front: Why does early-exit string comparison leak a secret?
cards.back: Response time grows with the number of correct leading bytes, letting attackers recover the secret byte-by-byte by picking the slowest candidate.

cards.front: How many requests to recover a 16-byte token via timing (256 guesses/byte)?
cards.back: 16 × 256 = 4096 — versus 256^16 by brute force.

cards.front: What does hmac.compare_digest do and when do you use it?
cards.back: Constant-time comparison of secret values — use for every token, HMAC, or hash comparison instead of ==.

cards.front: Flush+Reload in three steps?
cards.back: Flush a shared cache line, wait while victim runs, reload and time it — fast means the victim touched that line.

cards.front: What enables cache attacks across VMs?
cards.back: Shared hardware (CPU cache) and often shared memory pages between co-resident tenants.

cards.front: SPA vs DPA?
cards.back: SPA: one power trace, visually read (e.g., square-vs-multiply). DPA: many traces + statistics correlating guessed intermediates with measured power.

cards.front: What is blinding (RSA example)?
cards.back: Randomize the computation — multiply by a random value before the secret operation, remove it after — so the side channel carries no stable secret.

cards.front: What is masking?
cards.back: Split each sensitive value into random shares processed separately, so no single observable signal carries the secret.

cards.front: Why is added random delay not a complete timing defense?
cards.back: Statistics defeat noise with enough samples — it's defense-in-depth; constant-time code is the real fix.

cards.front: Are Spectre/Meltdown side-channel attacks? In what sense?
cards.back: Yes — at root they are cache side channels: speculation makes secret-dependent data touch the cache, and cache timing reads it out.

cards.front: Operator's three side-channel habits?
cards.back: Constant-time secret comparison in review, constant-time vetted crypto libraries, rate-limiting plus alerting on auth-oracle probing.

quiz.q: A token check returns False at the first mismatched byte. An attacker measures response times over many samples. What can they learn?
choices: Each correct leading byte, recovering the token byte-by-byte
Nothing — network jitter makes timing useless
quiz.explain: Early exit makes timing proportional to correct prefix length. Statistics (many samples, medians) defeat jitter — this is the canonical remote timing attack, fixed by constant-time comparison.

quiz.q: Why is hmac.compare_digest preferable to == for checking an API token?
choices: It compares in constant time — examining every byte regardless of mismatches
It hashes both sides with SHA-256
quiz.explain: compare_digest accumulates differences over all bytes and decides once, so timing reveals nothing about where (or whether) a mismatch occurred.

quiz.q: In Flush+Reload, a fast reload of the shared line tells the attacker…
choices: The victim accessed that memory line (it's back in cache)
quiz.explain: Cache residency is the signal: fast = someone (the victim) pulled the line back in. Repeating across lines and time reconstructs victim behavior.

quiz.q: RSA square-and-multiply leaks the key under SPA because…
choices: Multiply executes only for 1-bits, and squares vs multiplies look different on a power trace
The key is transmitted in the clear
quiz.explain: Key-dependent control flow is the leak: the operation sequence itself encodes the bits. Fix: key-independent operation sequences (e.g., Montgomery ladder).

quiz.q: DPA defeats simple dummy-operation defenses because…
choices: Statistics across many traces separate the real signal from the noise
quiz.explain: DPA correlates predicted intermediate values against thousands of traces; random dummy ops don't correlate with the key guess, so they average out. Masking (breaking the correlation) is the real defense.

quiz.q: Which defense directly breaks DPA's statistical correlation?
choices: Masking — secrets are split into random shares
quiz.explain: Masking ensures no single observable signal is a deterministic function of the secret, so the attacker's predicted intermediates don't correlate with measurements.

quiz.q: Your code does constant-time comparison but AES via key-dependent table lookups. Which side channel remains?
choices: Cache timing — table indices still depend on the key
quiz.explain: Constant-time must hold in every observable dimension. Key-dependent memory accesses leak via cache even when branch timing is flat — use AES-NI or bitsliced implementations.

quiz.q: An auth endpoint sees 5,000 rapid sequential token guesses from one IP with steadily increasing response times. Best response?
choices: Rate-limit/block, alert, verify constant-time comparison, consider rotating the token
Ignore it — timing attacks don't work over networks
Add a random delay and move on
quiz.explain: This is the exact signature of a timing-oracle campaign. Contain (block), verify the code-level fix exists, and rotate potentially-exposed secrets. Random delay alone is not a fix.

quiz.q: Why do cloud providers offer dedicated hosts / single-tenant hardware as a security option?
choices: Shared silicon enables cache side channels between co-resident tenants
quiz.explain: Cache attacks need co-residency. Removing the shared-cache neighbor removes the observation point — tenancy is a side-channel control.

handsOnLab.title: Timing oracle: build it, exploit it, fix it
handsOnLab.brief: Implement a naive early-exit token comparison and a constant-time version in Python, measure both with perf_counter to demonstrate the timing leak, then exploit the naive version to recover a token byte-by-byte and confirm the fixed version leaks nothing.
steps: Create timing_lab.py with insecure_compare (early exit) and secure_compare (XOR-accumulate, decide once).
Write a measure(fn, candidate, trials=2000) helper using time.perf_counter around each call; return the median.
Pick a random 8-byte secret. For the insecure version, time candidates matching 0..7 leading bytes; plot or print medians — confirm time grows with correct prefix length.
Write exploit(): for each position, try all 256 byte values (200 trials each), pick the slowest as the correct byte; recover the full secret and assert it matches.
Count total comparisons used and note the math: 8 x 256 vs 256^8 brute force.
Run the same measurement against secure_compare: confirm medians are flat regardless of correct prefix length.
Add random network-style jitter (time.sleep with small random) to measurements; show exploit still works with more trials (raise trials to 5000) — demonstrating why noise alone fails.
Replace secure_compare's core with hmac.compare_digest and re-verify flat timing.
Write timing-report.md: the leak mechanism, your measured numbers (fast vs slow medians), exploit request count, why the fix works, and where you'd look for this pattern in real code.
Grep one of your own projects (or Juice Shop's JS) for == comparisons on tokens/secrets and note any findings in the report.
handsOnLab.deliverable: timing_lab.py (vulnerable + fixed + exploit) and timing-report.md with measured medians and the fix rationale.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Your exploit recovers the 8-byte secret via the naive compare, and the constant-time version shows flat medians across all prefix lengths.

notes.title: Storing passwords: salts, work factors, and slow hashes
notes.body:
Never store passwords. Store the output of a password hashing function applied to the password plus a unique random salt, with a tunable work factor. Each piece defeats a specific attack.

The salt — a unique random value per user, stored alongside the hash — defeats rainbow tables (precomputed hash dictionaries). Without salts, an attacker who steals the user table precomputes one dictionary and cracks every common password instantly; with unique salts, they must attack each user individually. Salts don't need to be secret; they need to be unique and unpredictable.

The work factor (cost parameter) makes each guess expensive: the hash function is deliberately slow — hundreds of milliseconds per attempt. Legitimate logins pay this once; an attacker guessing billions of passwords pays it billions of times. And it's tunable: as hardware gets faster, you raise the cost at next login to keep pace.

The algorithm must be a password hashing function, not a general hash: bcrypt (adaptive cost, based on Blowfish, decades of scrutiny) and Argon2 (the Password Hashing Competition winner; memory-hard, so GPUs and ASICs gain little advantage) are the modern answers. Memory-hardness matters because attackers crack with parallel hardware — a function needing 64MB of RAM per guess cripples GPU farms that thrive on tiny, parallel computations. SHA-256(password) — even salted — is wrong: it's built for speed, and a single GPU tries billions of SHA-256 guesses per second.

Worked design: on registration, generate a 128-bit random salt, compute hash = Argon2(password, salt, time_cost, memory_cost), store (salt, parameters, hash). On login, recompute with the stored salt and parameters, compare with a constant-time comparison (M19's lesson — yes, password-hash comparison needs it too). If the work factor is now below policy, re-hash transparently at this login. Common failures: one global salt (rainbow tables work again), unsalted fast hashes (breach = instant mass compromise), encrypting passwords instead of hashing (key theft decrypts everything; hashing is one-way), and truncating passwords before hashing (silently weakens them).

Two advanced storage topics complete the picture. First, peppers: a secret value (stored separately from the database, e.g., in an HSM or config management) mixed into every hash. If the database is stolen but the pepper isn't, the hashes are useless — it converts a DB breach from catastrophe to incident. Peppers don't replace salts (they're not per-user) and they must be rotatable, but they're cheap defense-in-depth for high-value systems. Second, hash migration: you'll inherit unsalted MD5 or SHA-1 password tables. Don't force a mass reset on day one — instead, wrap: on next login, verify against the old hash, then immediately re-hash with Argon2 and discard the old. Within months of natural logins, the weak hashes are gone without a single user complaint. On Argon2 parameters: you'll see time cost, memory cost, and parallelism — raise memory cost first (that's what hurts GPUs), keep login time under roughly half a second so users don't notice, and re-tune every couple of years as hardware improves.

notes.title: Attack patterns: stuffing, spraying, and the reuse catastrophe
notes.body:
Attackers rarely 'hack' passwords; they reuse them. Know the three industrial patterns:

Credential stuffing: take username/password pairs from one breach and try them everywhere else. It works because humans reuse passwords across sites. Defenses: breach-correlation (check new passwords against known-breach lists at registration — 'have I been pwned'-style APIs exist for exactly this), device/behavioral risk signals, and MFA, which makes a stuffed password insufficient alone.

Password spraying: try a few common passwords (Spring2026!, Company123) against many accounts, staying under lockout thresholds. It's the inverse of brute force — low and slow across the user base instead of fast against one account. Defenses: lockouts and throttling keyed on the source as well as the account (spraying distributes across accounts precisely to dodge per-account lockout), alerting on the pattern (many accounts, few passwords, one source), and blocking the top-known passwords outright.

Brute force and dictionary attacks: systematic guessing against one account or one stolen hash. Against a live login, rate limiting and lockouts bound this; against a stolen hash database, only the work factor and password strength stand between the attacker and plaintext — which is why slow hashes and real password policies matter.

The operator's lens: your auth logs tell you which pattern is hitting you. Many failures, one account, one source = brute force. Few failures each, many accounts, one source = spraying. Successful logins from stuffed credentials look exactly like legitimate logins — that's why you need MFA and anomaly detection (M23), not just failure counting. And every one of these patterns is an argument you can take to leadership for MFA budget: passwords alone are a single factor defending against industrialized guessing.

Two more patterns round out the attacker's playbook. SIM-swap-to-SSO-takeover: the attacker ports the victim's number (social-engineering the carrier), receives the SMS MFA codes, and walks into every account where SMS is the second factor — email first, then password resets everywhere else. The chain works because SMS was the weakest link in an otherwise decent setup; the defense is removing SMS from the chain (TOTP or FIDO2) and putting carrier-level protections (port-out PINs) on important numbers. Helpdesk social engineering: the attacker calls support claiming to be the user, armed with public-record details, and gets a password reset. The defense is verification procedure — call back on a known number, require non-public verifiers, and log every reset for the user to see. Your detection queries should cover all three industrial patterns plus these: alert on password resets followed immediately by MFA enrollment changes (account takeover in progress), and on logins where the MFA method was just changed (the attacker swapped in their own factor).

notes.title: MFA: what the factors are and which ones actually help
notes.body:
Multi-factor authentication combines independent categories: something you know (password), something you have (phone, hardware key), something you are (biometrics). The security comes from independence — compromising one factor shouldn't compromise the others.

TOTP (time-based one-time passwords, the 6-digit codes in authenticator apps): the server and your app share a secret established at enrollment (usually via QR code). Both compute code = truncate(HMAC(secret, floor(now / 30s))). The 30-second time step means codes rotate; the server accepts the current and adjacent windows to tolerate clock skew. Worked implication: anyone holding the shared secret can generate valid codes — so the enrollment QR/code is itself a credential (screenshot it = clone the factor), and server-side the secret must be stored encrypted. TOTP resists replay (codes expire) and remote guessing, but it does NOT resist phishing: a fake login page can relay your password and your current code to the real site in real time.

SMS codes are the weakest common factor: SIM-swap attacks (social-engineering the carrier to port your number) hand the attacker your codes, and SMS is plaintext over SS7-era infrastructure. Use TOTP or better over SMS everywhere you have a choice; keep SMS only as a last-resort recovery path, and protect recovery paths as carefully as login paths — attackers target the weakest link, which is usually 'forgot my authenticator.'

Push-based MFA (approve/deny prompts) improved usability but introduced push fatigue: attackers spam prompts until the tired user taps Approve. Number matching (the login screen shows 'enter 47' and the push asks for the number) defeats blind approval. The ranking for new deployments: phishing-resistant factors (FIDO2) first, TOTP second, push with number matching third, SMS last. Rollout order as an operator: administrators and privileged accounts first (they're the highest-value targets), then everyone.

The enrollment ceremony deserves as much care as the login, because whoever enrolls the factor owns the account. For TOTP, the QR code or setup key is a credential — display it once, require immediate verification (enter two consecutive codes), and warn the user that screenshots clone the factor. For FIDO2, registration binds the new credential to the verified session: require the existing strong factor (or in-person proofing for first enrollment), show the user what they're approving ('add security key to your account?'), and register the credential's metadata so support can identify it later. Backup codes — the recovery factor — should be generated at enrollment, shown once, and stored hashed server-side like passwords (they're bearer credentials). A deployment detail that saves incidents: let users name their factors ('YubiKey — laptop bag') and show last-used times; when the 3 AM login comes from an unnamed factor, both the user and your analysts have context. Enrollment is authentication's front door — guard it like one.

notes.title: FIDO2 and passkeys: phishing-resistant authentication
notes.body:
FIDO2 (WebAuthn + CTAP) replaces shared secrets with public-key cryptography, and passkeys are its consumer-friendly form: the private key lives on the user's device (phone, laptop, hardware key), and the server stores only the public key. There is nothing to phish, nothing to stuff, and nothing valuable in a server breach.

The ceremony, step by step. Registration: the server sends a challenge (random nonce) plus its identity (the origin, e.g., login.example.com). The device generates a fresh keypair scoped to that origin, stores the private key, and returns the public key plus a signature over the challenge. Login: the server sends a new challenge; the device signs it with the origin-scoped private key (after a local gesture — biometrics or PIN — proving user presence); the server verifies the signature with the stored public key.

Why this resists phishing — the worked attack: the attacker builds a pixel-perfect fake at login-examp1e.com and you 'log in' with your passkey. Your device checks the origin: the credential was registered for login.example.com, and the challenge comes from login-examp1e.com. The origins don't match, so the device refuses to sign. There is no code for you to be tricked into relaying, unlike TOTP. The phishing page gets nothing — not a password, not a one-time code, not a signature valid anywhere else. Origin binding is the whole game, and it's enforced by the device, not by user vigilance.

Passkeys add syncability: platform vendors sync the private keys across a user's devices via their cloud account (protected by the account's own authentication), which solves the 'lost my hardware key' problem that stalled earlier FIDO deployments at the cost of making the platform account the new crown jewel. Discoverable credentials (usernameless login) let the device offer accounts directly. Operator considerations: plan account recovery before rollout (what happens when someone loses all devices?), keep a fallback factor for edge cases, and know that passkeys don't fix authorization — they prove who, not what they're allowed to do.

Two passkey deployment realities to plan for. First, synced vs device-bound: platform passkeys sync across the user's devices via their cloud account (convenient; the cloud account becomes the crown jewel — protect it with its own phishing-resistant MFA), while security keys and some platform configurations keep keys on one device (stronger; loss means recovery flow). Enterprises often want the latter for privileged accounts and accept the former for general users — a tiered policy, documented. Second, attestation: during registration, the authenticator can provide an attestation statement about its make and model, letting the server enforce 'only certified hardware keys for admins.' Use attestation as an allowlist ('these models permitted'), not a denylist, and have a process for new models. Recovery remains the hard part: with no passwords to reset, losing all devices means a rigorous identity-proofing flow (document verification, manager approval, cooldown with alerts to backup contacts). Design and test this flow before rollout — the first real recovery shouldn't be improvised during an incident.

notes.title: Failure patterns: how authentication breaks in practice
notes.body:
Authentication failures follow a depressing set of patterns. Learn them in general terms so you recognize each on sight:

Plaintext or reversible storage: the breach doesn't just expose accounts, it exposes every password for stuffing elsewhere. The fix was decided decades ago — salted slow hashes — yet audits still find plaintext. Your review checklist starts here.

Missing or optional MFA on privileged accounts: attackers don't target average users first; they target admins, finance, and IT. Every privileged account without phishing-resistant MFA is the incident waiting to happen. Rollout order is a security decision: admins, then executives (whaling targets), then everyone.

Weak recovery flows: 'answer your security questions' (answers are public records or guessable), SMS fallback on an otherwise strong setup, helpdesk password resets without identity verification. Attackers enumerate the paths to an account and take the weakest — your authentication is only as strong as its recovery procedure. Design recovery with the same rigor as login: verified out-of-band channels, cooldowns, and alerting to the legitimate user.

Session flaws after good authentication: fixation (M17), overlong lifetimes, no invalidation on password change. Authenticating strongly and then handing out a forever-token wastes the effort.

Credential exposure in logs and errors: passwords in application logs, tokens in URLs (logged by proxies), verbose 'user not found' vs 'wrong password' distinctions that enable username enumeration. Log auth events richly (who, when, from where, result) but never log the secrets themselves.

The meta-pattern: each failure is a place where one link was weaker than the rest. Your job is to walk the whole chain — storage, factors, recovery, session, logging — and bring the weakest link up, because attackers don't attack your strongest control.

Three more failure patterns to file away. Session flaws after strong auth: the login was FIDO2-grade, but the session cookie lives for a year and never rotates — the attacker who steals it (via malware, not phishing) bypasses everything. Match session strength to auth strength: strong auth deserves short, rotated, well-flagged sessions (M17's design). OAuth and token leakage: 'login with' integrations and API tokens get logged in URLs, committed to repos, and pasted into tickets — each is a bearer credential as powerful as a password. Scan for them (secret scanning exists for exactly this), scope them narrowly, and rotate on any exposure. Default and shared credentials: the appliance with admin/admin, the team sharing one 'deploy' account — no MFA scheme survives a password everyone knows. Eliminate shared accounts (named accounts with individual MFA, plus break-glass accounts sealed and monitored), because every pattern in this module assumes you know which human authenticated — shared credentials destroy that assumption at the root.

notes.title: The operator's authentication checklist
notes.body:
Turn the module into an actionable checklist you can run against any system you inherit:

Password policy that actually works: require length (12+ characters; passphrases welcome), check against breach lists and trivial variants at set time, and stop demanding arbitrary complexity rules and 90-day rotations — the evidence has long shown those produce Password1! → Password2! patterns. Complexity theater is worse than useless because it consumes goodwill.

Storage audit: confirm salted slow hashes (bcrypt/Argon2) with a current work factor; confirm no plaintext, no unsalted fast hashes, no reversible encryption of passwords; confirm constant-time comparison on verification.

MFA posture: enumerate every privileged account and confirm phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys/FIDO2) or at minimum TOTP; eliminate SMS where possible; document and harden recovery paths; enable number matching on push.

Session hygiene: fresh random ids at login, Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite flags, absolute plus idle timeouts, invalidation on logout and password change (M17's design).

Monitoring: alert on spraying patterns (many accounts, few passwords, one source), stuffing indicators (logins from breached-credential intelligence), impossible-travel and new-device logins, MFA fatigue (many pushes, one approval), and recovery-flow abuse. Feed these into your detection thinking from M23: authentication telemetry is your richest behavioral feature source.

Interview bridge: ThreatLocker's Elevation Control removes standing local admin and grants just-in-time elevation per application via policy — that's authentication-adjacent least privilege on the endpoint. When the panel asks how you'd secure admin access, you now have the full stack: strong auth to prove who, MFA to prove it's really them, and just-in-time elevation so the privilege exists only when needed.

Turn the checklist into a rollout plan with metrics. Phase one — privileged accounts: enumerate every admin, service, and break-glass account; require phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys/security keys); eliminate SMS; document and test recovery. Metric: percentage of privileged accounts with phishing-resistant MFA — target 100%, reported weekly until it holds. Phase two — general users: TOTP minimum, passkeys offered and encouraged, SMS deprecated with a sunset date. Metric: MFA coverage and factor-strength distribution. Phase three — continuous: monitor the detection queries from the attack-patterns note, run a tabletop exercise ('the CFO's phone with the authenticator is stolen at 9 PM — walk through recovery'), and audit enrollment and reset logs quarterly. Report to leadership in risk terms: 'account-takeover expected loss reduced by X, remaining gap is Y.' And keep the human factor in view: the smoothest MFA rollout still fails if the helpdesk reset procedure is one phone call with public details — verify the recovery path with the same rigor as the login path, because attackers will.

cards.front: Why must password hashes use a unique salt per user?
cards.back: Defeats rainbow tables — attackers must attack each user's hash individually instead of precomputing one dictionary for all.

cards.front: What is a work factor / cost parameter?
cards.back: Tunable slowness in the hash function: legitimate logins pay it once, attackers pay it per guess. Raised over time as hardware improves.

cards.front: bcrypt vs Argon2 — one line each?
cards.back: bcrypt: adaptive-cost Blowfish-based hash, long scrutiny history. Argon2: memory-hard PHC winner — resists GPU/ASIC cracking.

cards.front: Why is SHA-256(password) wrong even when salted?
cards.back: It's designed for speed — GPUs try billions of guesses/sec. Password hashing must be deliberately slow and memory-hard.

cards.front: Credential stuffing vs password spraying?
cards.back: Stuffing: breached pairs tried everywhere (exploits reuse). Spraying: few common passwords tried against many accounts (dodges per-account lockout).

cards.front: How does TOTP work (three parts)?
cards.back: Shared secret + HMAC over floor(time/30s), truncated to digits. Server and app compute the same code independently.

cards.front: Why is SMS the weakest MFA factor?
cards.back: SIM-swap attacks port the number to the attacker; SMS travels over legacy signaling infrastructure in the clear.

cards.front: What is push fatigue and its fix?
cards.back: Spamming approve/deny prompts until the user taps Approve. Fix: number matching — the push asks for the number shown on the login screen.

cards.front: FIDO2/passkeys in one sentence?
cards.back: Origin-scoped public-key challenge-response: the device signs the server's challenge with a private key that never leaves it.

cards.front: Why are passkeys phishing-resistant?
cards.back: Origin binding: the device only signs challenges from the registered origin, so a fake site gets no usable signature — nothing to relay.

cards.front: What's the usual weakest link in an MFA deployment?
cards.back: Account recovery — SMS fallback, security questions, or helpdesk resets weaker than the login flow itself.

cards.front: Effective password policy in one line?
cards.back: Length over complexity, breach-list checks at set time, no forced rotation theater.

quiz.q: An attacker steals a user table hashed with unsalted SHA-256. What happens next?
choices: One precomputed rainbow table cracks common passwords for all users almost instantly
Each user must be attacked individually
quiz.explain: No salts = one dictionary serves every row; fast hash = billions of guesses/sec. This is exactly the catastrophe salts plus work factors prevent.

quiz.q: Why is Argon2's memory-hardness valuable against attackers?
choices: GPUs/ASICs excel at tiny parallel computations; forcing 64MB+ per guess cripples their advantage
It removes the need for salts
quiz.explain: Cracking economics: attackers win with massively parallel cheap hardware. Memory-hardness changes the cost equation against them while legitimate servers pay it once per login.

quiz.q: Logs show 3 failed logins each across 2,000 accounts from one IP, using 'Welcome2026!'. This pattern is…
choices: Password spraying — throttle by source, alert on the pattern, block common passwords
A brute-force attack on one account
quiz.explain: Few passwords × many accounts × one source, deliberately under per-account lockout thresholds = spraying. Per-account lockout alone won't catch it.

quiz.q: A phishing page relays the victim's password AND current TOTP code to the real site in real time. Why does this work against TOTP but fail against passkeys?
choices: TOTP codes are bearer values valid during their window; passkeys are origin-bound signatures unusable on the wrong origin
Phishing pages can't display TOTP prompts
quiz.explain: A TOTP code is a string anyone can forward within 30 seconds. A passkey signature is bound to the real origin by the device itself — the fake origin gets nothing usable.

quiz.q: During FIDO2 login, what does the server verify?
choices: A signature over its fresh challenge, made by the private key matching the registered public key, for the correct origin
That the user typed a password
quiz.explain: Challenge-response: fresh challenge defeats replay, origin binding defeats phishing, public-key crypto means the server never holds a phishable secret.

quiz.q: An admin account has a 20-character random password but no MFA. An intern account has MFA. Which is the priority fix?
choices: The admin account — privileged targets are attacked first; password strength doesn't replace a second factor
The intern account — interns click phishing links
quiz.explain: Attackers target privilege, not password length. MFA rollout order is a security decision: admins and high-value targets first.

quiz.q: Your app says 'username not found' vs 'wrong password' distinctly. What's the issue?
choices: Username enumeration — attackers can harvest valid accounts for spraying/stuffing
quiz.explain: Distinct errors are an oracle for account existence. Use one generic 'login failed' message; log specifics server-side.

quiz.q: After a password change, old sessions stay valid. Why is this wrong?
choices: A compromised session survives the remediation — password changes must invalidate all sessions
quiz.explain: Password reset is incident response for the account. Leaving sessions alive leaves the attacker's access alive — 'log me out everywhere' must be real.

quiz.q: Which comparison is correct for verifying a password-reset token in Python?
quiz.explain: M19's lesson applied: secret comparison must be constant-time. == leaks via early exit; compare_digest doesn't.

quiz.q: A deployment uses push MFA without number matching. Users report 3 AM approval prompts. Diagnosis and fix?
choices: Push fatigue attack — enable number matching, alert on prompt bursts, investigate the source
Normal behavior — tell users to approve
quiz.explain: Prompt-bombing at 3 AM is an attacker hoping for a half-asleep tap. Number matching makes blind approval useless; bursts are a detection signal.

items.prompt: Three ingredients of proper password storage?
items.answer: Unique salt per user, slow hash (bcrypt/Argon2), tunable work factor.
items.explain: Salt defeats rainbow tables; slowness defeats guessing; tuning keeps pace with hardware.

items.prompt: Why not SHA-256 for passwords?
items.answer: Built for speed — billions of guesses/sec on GPUs.
items.explain: Password hashing must be deliberately slow and memory-hard.

items.prompt: Stuffing vs spraying in one line each?
items.answer: Stuffing: breached pairs reused everywhere. Spraying: common passwords vs many accounts.
items.explain: Different patterns, different detections.

items.prompt: TOTP's three ingredients?
items.answer: Shared secret, HMAC, 30-second time step.
items.explain: Both sides compute the same rotating code independently.

items.prompt: Why does TOTP fall to real-time phishing?
items.answer: The code is a bearer value — anyone can relay it within its window.
items.explain: No origin binding, unlike FIDO2.

items.prompt: The phishing-resistance mechanism in passkeys?
items.answer: Origin binding — the device signs only for the registered origin.
items.explain: A fake origin receives no usable signature.

items.prompt: First accounts to get phishing-resistant MFA?
items.answer: Administrators and privileged accounts.
items.explain: Attackers target privilege first.

items.prompt: Scenario: breach of a competitor's forum; next day your login success rate spikes from unusual IPs. Diagnosis and response?
items.answer: Credential stuffing with the breached pairs; force MFA challenges on risky logins, check passwords against breach lists, alert users to rotate reused passwords.
items.explain: Successes that look legitimate are the stuffing signature — failure counting won't see them.

items.prompt: Scenario: helpdesk resets passwords over the phone with only 'name and employee ID' as verification. Finding?
items.answer: Recovery weaker than login — public/guessable verifier; require verified out-of-band identity proof and alert the user.
items.explain: Attackers take the weakest path to the account.

items.prompt: Scenario: choosing between SMS codes and TOTP for a new internal app. Recommendation?
items.answer: TOTP minimum; prefer passkeys. SMS only as last-resort recovery, never primary.
items.explain: SIM-swap defeats SMS; TOTP resists replay; passkeys resist phishing.

items.prompt: Scenario: user loses the phone with their authenticator and there's no recovery process. What should have existed?
items.answer: Pre-planned recovery: backup codes issued at enrollment, verified out-of-band reset with cooldown and user alerting.
items.explain: Design recovery with login-grade rigor before rollout, not during the incident.

items.prompt: Scenario: code review finds password comparison with ==. Fix and why?
items.answer: hmac.compare_digest — == is an early-exit timing oracle on the hash.
items.explain: M19 applied: secret comparison is always constant-time.

items.prompt: Scenario: the panel asks how you'd secure local admin on endpoints. Tie this module to ThreatLocker.
items.answer: Strong auth + phishing-resistant MFA to prove identity, then Elevation Control for just-in-time per-app elevation — privilege exists only when needed, no standing admin.
items.explain: Authentication proves who; just-in-time elevation limits what that who can do.

handsOnLab.title: Password hashing and TOTP in pure Python
handsOnLab.brief: Build a correct password registration/login flow with hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac (stdlib), then implement TOTP from RFC 6238 primitives and validate it against the RFC's published test vectors.
steps: Create auth_lab.py. Implement register(password): generate 16 random bytes via secrets.token_bytes, derive with hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', pw, salt, 600_000), store salt+iterations+derived.
Implement verify(password, record): recompute and compare with hmac.compare_digest. Confirm correct password passes, wrong fails.
Demonstrate the salt's job: register the same password twice; show the stored hashes differ.
Demonstrate the work factor: time 600k vs 60k iterations; compute attacker cost for a million guesses at each setting.
Write the 'never do' list as code comments: plaintext, unsalted SHA-256, global salt, == comparison.

Implement totp(secret, time_step=30, digits=8): counter = int(time.time())//30; msg = struct.pack('>Q', counter); hs = hmac.new(secret, msg, hashlib.sha1).digest(); dynamic-truncate per RFC 4226; mod 10^digits.
Validate against RFC 6238 Appendix B test vectors (secret '12345678901234567890'): fetch the expected values from the RFC text and assert your implementation matches at least two timestamps.
Simulate clock skew: verify your verifier accepts counters within ±1 step and rejects ±10 steps.
Write a phishing-relay thought experiment in comments: why a stolen TOTP code works within its window but a passkey signature for the wrong origin is useless.
Write auth-report.md: your measured hash timings, the TOTP validation results, and the operator checklist applied to one real account you own (MFA status, recovery path).
handsOnLab.deliverable: auth_lab.py (hasher + TOTP + RFC validation) and auth-report.md with timings, validation results, and a personal MFA/recovery audit.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Same password yields different stored hashes; TOTP output matches the RFC 6238 test vectors; your report names the recovery path for your own most important account.

mockTask.q: Panel question: we're rolling out MFA to 500 endpoints. The team proposes SMS codes because 'everyone has a phone.' What's your recommendation?
